name: Lotus Tower
label: Lotus Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/728831229: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Colombo Lotus Tower' (118 m across).
notes: Lotus-shaped tower, the tallest structure in South Asia.

text.description: The Lotus Tower, also called the Colombo Lotus Tower, is a slender, lotus-shaped tower beside Beira Lake. It stands 351.5 metres tall, and as of 2019 it was the tallest self-supported structure in South Asia. The design takes its shape from the lotus flower, which in Sri Lankan culture stands for purity, and the base echoes a lotus throne. That simple, recognisable outline is what makes it work so well in a photo: one tall shape against the sky, with the lake and city around it. Its lights can change colour, so an evening visit can give you a very different picture from a daytime one. Work was under way from January 2012, and the opening ceremony was held on 16 September 2019. The tower carries broadcasting antennas and also has visitor facilities, including an observation gallery. The phone icon on the map sits at the middle of the tower, within or beside its base area, so you will be near its base, looking up. For the full shape, walk back a little along the waterfront until the whole tower fits in the frame. Keep the phone upright and level so the sides stay straight. Try one wide shot with the lake or some foreground, and one close shot of the textured base. People walking past can give a useful sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: The Lotus Tower is in Colombo 01, on the waterfront of Beira Lake, alongside D. R. Wijewardene Mawatha.
text.directions_text: Start from Colombo 01, the area around Beira Lake, and head to the tower. The Lotus Tower (Colombo Lotus Tower) is on the Beira Lake waterfront in Colombo 01. The phone icon on the map is at the middle of the tower, so once you reach the tower's base area you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because from close to the tower's base it is the only lens that fits much of the height into the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for tidier, less stretched shots once you step back. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it from a distance to pick out the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a full-height view, walk back along the waterfront until the whole tower fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Point the phone straight ahead rather than tilting it far upwards, then step back to get the top in. Use the lake or some paving as a foreground to add depth. For a bolder shot, hold the phone low and shoot the base against the sky with the ultra-wide.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the lights sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good choice, as the light softens and the tower's colour-changing lights can be seen against the darkening sky.

text.access_note: The area around the tower is a waterfront, but please check current access details before you go.

name: Pettah Market
label: Pettah Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Khan Clock Tower' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Khan Clock Tower' (node/3163979473): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7179273: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Busy bazaar district with colourful street trading.

text.description: Pettah Market, also known as Manning Market, is an open market in the Pettah district of Colombo. Its entrance is marked by the Khan Clock Tower, a tall monument standing in the middle of a roundabout. The tower was built by the family of Framjee Bhickajee Khan, a well-known Parsi family from Bombay who had large business interests in Sri Lanka and owned the Colombo Oil Mills. For a phone photographer it is a good place to begin. The tower gives you a clear upright subject, and the market entrance and the movement of people sit below it, so a single frame says 'this is where the market starts'. Stand across the street from the tower and fit both the tower and the crowd at its base into the picture. Once you have that shot, walk into the market for closer pictures. Inside, the open-air aisles have produce and goods with workers moving through, and Keyzer Street has older stalls with colourful displays arranged by type of goods. Ask before you photograph any vendor. According to one guide, Sunday retail is reduced and wholesale is closed, so weekdays or Saturday mornings give you the busiest scenes. Some maps may use a different name for the tower, so look for the roundabout.
text.geographic_location: In the Pettah district of Colombo, at the market entrance marked by the Khan Clock Tower on a roundabout. The market lies beyond the entrance.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the Khan Clock Tower in the Pettah area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the street so the whole tower and the crowd below it fit in. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or people stop you stepping back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face and stall details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (across the street from the tower, framing the market entrance below it). The four-storey clock tower with the market entrance and street activity beneath it, a clear marker for where the market begins. The best place to stand is across the street from the Khan Clock Tower at the market entrance, so the entrance is framed below the tower. Check the tower's exact position on the map when you arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one vertical line with the entrance and street activity along the bottom. Keep your phone upright so the full height of the tower fits. For a second view, walk into the market for open aisles of produce, or to Keyzer Street for older stalls and vendors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the people or stalls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky behind the tower does not wash out. Hold the shutter for a Live Photo to catch the street moving. Ask before photographing vendors.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekdays or Saturday mornings, when the market is busiest. Sunday is much quieter.

text.access_note: According to one guide, Sunday retail is reduced and wholesale is closed, so expect a quieter market on that day.

name: Galle Face Hotel
label: Galle Face Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Galle Face Green' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Galle Face Green' (way/27712165): edge nearest the subject (978 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1430312630: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galle Face Hotel' (236 m across).
notes: Colonial-era grand hotel facing the ocean.

text.description:
The Galle Face Hotel is a long, colonial-era seafront building on Galle Road, and it is one of the oldest hotels east of Suez. It was founded in 1864 by four British entrepreneurs and began as a Dutch villa called Galle Face House. It takes its name from Galle Face Green, the stretch of lawn it faces. The south wing, designed by the architect Edward Skinner, was completed in 1894. The property has stayed largely unchanged since then, apart from careful restorations, including a refurbishment of the north wing that finished in 2015.

It photographs well because of the setting. The old facade sits right beside the open lawn and the Indian Ocean, so one frame can hold history, grass, sky and sea. The best place for this is the northern end of Galle Face Green, where the promenade begins beside the hotel. From there the hotel's colonial front fills one side of the frame, with the ocean and the sea-facing lawn behind or beside it. It looks best as the light softens in the late afternoon.

Stay on the public green rather than going into the hotel grounds, as the hotel is private property. If you want a plain sunset over the water, walk further along the green. The hotel is not part of that view, but the open horizon, often with ships on it, is a good second shot. Leave a little sky above the roofline so the building has room.
text.geographic_location: The hotel is on Galle Road in Colombo, facing the long seafront lawn of Galle Face Green, with the Indian Ocean just beyond.
text.directions_text: The hotel is directly south of that point, about 1 minute on foot. Head for the green rather than the hotel entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long facade and the sea in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Galle Face Green (northern end, where the promenade begins beside the hotel). The hotel's colonial facade in the frame, with the ocean and the sea-facing lawn behind or beside it. The hotel lies to the south. From here you see its colonial facade in the frame, with the ocean and the sea-facing lawn behind or beside it. If you want an open sunset instead, with no hotel in the picture, walk further along the green; that view shows the Indian Ocean and often ships on the horizon.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of the horizontal lines so the sea sits level. Place the hotel on one side of the frame and let the lawn lead the eye towards it. Leave a little sky above the roofline. If the facade is too wide to fit, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Taking a few frames in quick succession helps when people walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 4 to 5 pm, when the light is softer and you can find a spot before the crowds build.

text.access_note: Galle Face Green is a public open space, but the hotel itself is private property, so take your photos from the green and check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the hotel's restaurants or museum.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps fit a long building and the sea into one frame from close range.
A level horizon and slightly lowered exposure usually improve a sunset-lit or bright-sky photo on a phone.
The hotel is south of the northern end of the green and the Indian Ocean lies to the west of it (sunset side).

name: Gangaramaya Temple
label: Gangaramaya Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gangaramaya Temple' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5521071: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Buddhist temple with a museum and ornate shrine halls.

text.description: Gangaramaya is one of Colombo's most important Buddhist temples, and it photographs well because there is so much packed into one compound. The architecture mixes Sri Lankan, Thai, Indian and Chinese styles. Inside the main image house, large seated Buddha images, decorated walls and ceilings and golden statues all compete for your attention. It was completed in the late 19th century on what began as a small hermitage on marshy land beside Beira Lake. The compound also has a stupa, a Bo tree grown from a sapling brought from Anuradhapura, a museum and a library. For a phone, the strongest picture is the interior of the main hall, looking from the entrance side towards the Buddha statues. It makes a quieter, more personal photo than the lakeside views. Morning light through the window screens can throw patterns across the floor, which adds depth to the shot. If you have time, Seema Malaka, the Geoffrey Bawa-designed pavilions on Beira Lake, makes a good second picture, with timber verandas reflected in the water. The stupa and Bo tree on their raised platform are another option. This is a working place of worship, so keep your phone low-key, avoid flash, and never pose with your back to a Buddha statue.
text.geographic_location: Gangaramaya Temple stands beside Beira Lake in Colombo, a short distance from the water's edge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Beira Lake area of Colombo and look for the temple compound beside the lake. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the temple itself, so there is no extra walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the full hall with the seated Buddhas and decorated ceiling. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a single statue or a detail of the walls. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for gold details that are further away, if you can't or shouldn't step closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the interior of the main hall, with its large seated Buddha images, decorated walls and ceilings, and the golden statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the walls and pillars straight to the lines, so the room doesn't lean. Put the biggest seated Buddha slightly off-centre, with the decorated ceiling filling the top of the frame. If you want a lake view as well, Seema Malaka on Beira Lake, with its reflections, makes a good alternative. Please do not pose with your back to a statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the face of a statue, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold doesn't wash out. Turn the flash off, as it is not welcome in shrines. If your phone switches to night mode in the dim interior, hold it steady with both hands, elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before the crowds build and while light filters through the window screens and makes patterns on the floor.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship: cover your shoulders and knees, expect to take off shoes and hats inside, and check the official site before you go for any entry or photo fees.

name: Galle Face Green
label: Galle Face Green
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Galle Face Green' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Galle Face Green' (way/27712165): edge nearest the subject (978 m across).
notes: Seafront promenade at sunset with the Indian Ocean and kite flyers.

text.description:
Galle Face Green is a long, open seafront lawn in the middle of Colombo, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to photograph a sunset. The park covers about 5 hectares and runs for roughly 500 metres along the coast. Its promenade was laid out in 1859 under Governor Sir Henry George Ward, and in the 1820s the green was used for horse racing. Today it is a place for kite flyers, picnickers and food vendors, and it is busiest on Saturday and Sunday evenings.

For photographs, the best spot is the southern tip, facing the open ocean. The horizon is clear there, ships sometimes pass, and kite flyers can fill the foreground. Guides suggest arriving about 15 minutes before sunset so you can settle in and try a few framings. If you want a quieter scene, Marine Drive offers long sea views with fewer people, and the Galle Face Hotel's colonial facade makes a backdrop as the light softens. Both are optional extras.

Be aware that the shore is rocky rather than sandy, and vendors and stray dogs gather on the lawn. Keep an eye on your phone and bag, and agree any tuk-tuk fare before you set off. Building work for the Port City is gradually changing the skyline.
text.geographic_location: Galle Face Green is in the heart of Colombo, on the seafront between Galle Road and the Indian Ocean. The Galle Face Hotel sits at one end of the green and the Ceylon Inter-Continental Hotel at the other.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Colombo and make your way to the seafront green by road. From there the main part of the green lies to the north-west, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sunset and horizon. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more sky and the kite flyers. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a passing ship on the horizon.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Galle Face Green (southern tip, facing the open ocean). Sunset over the Indian Ocean with the horizon unobstructed, sometimes with ships passing and kite flyers in the foreground. From here you look out over the Indian Ocean with a clear horizon, and the main stretch of the green lies off to your north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower or upper line so it stays level. If kite flyers are out, include one or two in the foreground for scale and colour. For a different view, try the Galle Face Hotel facade as a backdrop, or Marine Drive for a quieter sea view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the sun does not wash out. Try Live Photos for moving kites, and use night mode only once the light has nearly gone.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive about 15 minutes before sunset and stay through the last hour of daylight. Weekend evenings are busier.

text.access_note: The green is an open public park by the sea; check the official site before you go in case of events or restrictions.

name: Fort railway station
label: Fort Railway Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Colombo Fort Railway Station concourse' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/232514810: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Colombo Fort' (88 m across).
notes: Main railway terminus in Colombo, a hub for train trips.

text.description: Fort railway station is Colombo's main rail hub and the end of the line for most intercity trains in Sri Lanka. That makes it a good place for a phone photographer who likes everyday life: commuters crossing the concourse, food stalls, and trains pulling in under the station roof, with light falling through the roof onto the floor. The present station opened in 1917 on land reclaimed from the Beira Lake, and it was built along similar lines to Manchester Victoria station. The platforms run east to west, and the ticket hall sits to the north of them. The concourse is a quieter alternative to the colonial-era facade, and you can walk in without any fuss. From the phone icon on the map, you are inside the main concourse by the entrance, with the platforms nearby. Look for strong shafts of light, the rhythm of passengers walking past, and a train waiting at the platform. If you would like the outside view instead, the station's colonial-era front, with red brick walls and arched doorways, works well as part of the street scene. Be friendly and discreet: ask before you photograph anyone close up, keep out of the way of people with luggage, and be mindful of security staff.
text.geographic_location: Fort railway station is in the heart of Colombo, right next to the Fort district and the Pettah markets. Colombo Secretariat station is a short way to the west.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or Underground-style stops to give you, so start from Pettah or the Fort area, both right beside the station. The station is in central Colombo and is linked by rail, and by buses through the Central Bus Stand in Pettah. Once you are at the phone icon on the map there is no further walking to do. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for people, stalls and trains. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the station roof and the length of a platform. If you want a closer shot of a train or a stall from a respectful distance, try 2x telephoto, if your phone has it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can see commuters, food stalls and trains on the platforms under the roof, with light falling through the roof onto the floor.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the walkers or a train along one of the lines, with the light patch on the floor as your foreground. Wait for someone to walk into the light rather than chasing people. For a different view, the station's colonial-era front with its red brick walls and arched doorways makes a good second shot from the street side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: The light changes sharply between the shaded concourse and the bright areas. Tap to focus on a person or train, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit patches don't blow out. Try a Live Photo or short burst when a train arrives. Keep clear of the platform edge while you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives you the light coming through the roof. Fort is a major commuter hub, so expect crowds at busy times.

text.access_note: Visitors can generally walk into the station and photograph the platforms and stalls, but ask before photographing individuals, follow staff instructions, and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Daytime is the best time to see light falling through the roof.
Platform edges can be crowded, so it is sensible to keep clear of them while taking photos.
A telephoto lens (2x) is available only on some phones.

name: Jami Ul-Alfar Mosque
label: Red Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '2nd Cross Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of 2nd Cross Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/20279441: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Red Mosque' (75 m across).

text.description:
Jami Ul-Alfar, known locally as the Red Mosque, is one of the oldest mosques in Colombo. It stands on Second Cross Street in Pettah, and its red-and-white candy stripes stand out among the plainer buildings around it. It was built between 1908 and 1909 for the local Indian Muslim community. Its designer and builder, Habibu Lebbe Saibu Lebbe, worked from pictures and details of Indo-Saracenic buildings supplied by South Indian traders. The result mixes Indo-Islamic and Indian styles with Gothic revival and Neo-classical touches. In 1975 the mosque began an expansion intended to raise its capacity to 10,000 worshippers.

It photographs well because the pattern is strong and simple: bands of colour, domes, minarets and a clock tower, all facing the street. The best picture is the whole front facade, taken from across the street. From there the mosque is to the east of you. Stand opposite the front, keep your phone upright and level, and let the stripes fill the frame. For a second view, Petra Road is suggested for seeing the mosque from a distance against the neighbouring buildings, but check the exact street on the map first. Morning light is said to suit the facade best. This is a working place of worship, so keep your photos respectful and be ready to move aside for people going in.
text.geographic_location: The mosque is in Pettah, Colombo, on Second Cross Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby, so start from Pettah and head for 2nd Cross Street. Ask for the Red Mosque (Jami Ul-Alfar). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole striped facade, domes and minarets into one frame from across the street. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view if you can step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes, the clock tower and the stripe patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 2nd Cross Street (opposite side of the street from the mosque's front facade). The full red-and-white striped front facade with its domes and minarets, framed against the street. From there the full red-and-white striped front, with its domes and minarets, is framed against the street. The mosque lies to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with them, so the minarets don't lean. Keep the phone level and raise it a little if people or vehicles block the base. For a different picture, Petra Road is suggested as a place to see the mosque from a distance, set against the surrounding buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stripes keep their detail and the red stays rich. Use the 0.5x lens for the full front, and switch to 2x or more for details rather than pinch-zooming.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun is said to light the facade well. Avoid prayer times, including Friday around noon.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly with covered arms and legs, avoid prayer times, and check visiting and prayer times locally before going if you hope to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The street in front of the mosque is likely to be busy with people and vehicles, so you may need to wait for a clear view.
The ultra-wide lens helps when you cannot step far back from the facade.
Bright light can wash out white stripes, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
Women may be restricted from the inner areas of the mosque, and you should ask before photographing people.

name: Colombo National Museum
label: National Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138991604: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum of Colombo' (154 m across).
notes: Sri Lanka's largest museum in a white colonial building.

text.description:
The Colombo National Museum is the largest museum in Sri Lanka. It opened in 1877 and holds important collections, including the regalia of the Kandyan monarchs and the throne of the last king of Kandy. The building was designed by the government architect James George Smither in the Italian style and finished in 1876. That style gives it a formal, symmetrical front, which suits a phone camera well. Straight lines, steps, columns and arches all sit comfortably in a single frame.

The building is wide, so the main task is fitting it in. Stepping back and using the ultra-wide (0.5x) lets you take in the whole front, but keep it level. Switch on the gridlines and line them up with the roofline or the base of the walls, so the edges don't lean inwards. For a tighter shot, use the default lens (1x) and pick out one detail, such as an arch, a doorway or a row of windows. If people are walking past, wait a moment and take the photo when they are small in the frame. They also show how big the building is.

The museum has a library as well, founded in the same year, which shows how much the place has grown since 1877. Inside, you may find displays and rules about photography that differ from the grounds, so ask or check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Colombo, Sri Lanka.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi or hired scooter from central Colombo. Ask for the Colombo National Museum by name. When you arrive, use the map to walk to the phone icon on the map. The building is large, so allow a few minutes to move around for different views, where access allows. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole width of the building in. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as carved stonework, window frames or a doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Treat it as your starting point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the roofline or the base of the walls with a horizontal line, so the building looks straight. Keep the phone level and don't tilt it upwards, or the walls will lean inwards. For a second picture, move in and frame one arch or doorway in the default lens (1x), with a little of the surrounding wall around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the front looks washed out. If the building is in shade and the sky is bright, tap the wall instead so it doesn't turn dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the front of a building than the middle of the day. Thin cloud also works well because it avoids harsh shadows under the roof and arches.

text.access_note: The grounds and the museum may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go for access and any rules on photography inside.

name: Viharamahadevi Park
label: Viharamahadevi Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Viharamahadevi Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Viharamahadevi Park Aquarium' (node/10107520123): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/22323428: large area 'Vihara Maha Devi Park' (851 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Largest park in Colombo with a golden Buddha statue.

text.description: Viharamahadevi Park is Colombo's oldest and largest park, and its open lawns make a calm foreground for one of the city's best-known civic scenes: the white Neo-Classical Town Hall just across the road. The British built it as Victoria Park, and it was renamed after Queen Viharamahadevi on 18 July 1958. It was occupied by the British Army during the Second World War and opened to the public again in 1951. Today it is looked after by the Colombo Municipal Council. The park is also known for a large Buddha statue, which replaced the statue of Queen Victoria that originally stood there, and for its water fountains. Ducks swim on the artificial lake and wander the grass beside it. The Cenotaph War Memorial and the Colombo Public Library are at the western end. For most visitors the easiest photo is the Town Hall seen over the grass from the park's edge. Keep the building centred, use the lawn as a wide, green foreground, and wait for a gap in the people if you want a clean frame. If you have time to walk further in, the Buddha statue with its gardens and fountains is the park's best-known landmark. The lily pond, with banyan trees around it, is a softer and quieter scene. Late afternoon is the time guides recommend for the Town Hall view.
text.geographic_location: The park is in Cinnamon Gardens, in central Colombo, directly in front of the colonial-era Town Hall. The Cenotaph War Memorial and the Colombo Public Library are at its western end.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Town Hall in Cinnamon Gardens. From there the subject is about 143 m (a short walk) to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Town Hall across the lawns. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more grass and sky, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the building's details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Viharamahadevi Park (lawns on the side facing the Town Hall across the road). The white Neo-Classical Colombo Town Hall framed by the park's open lawns, the classic civic-scene view. From here the white Neo-Classical Town Hall sits framed by the park's open lawns.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Town Hall on the centre line, with the lawn filling the lower third. Keep your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight. For a different picture, walk in to the gold-toned Buddha statue with its gardens and fountains, or to the lily pond with banyan trees, which suits a quieter, softer shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so it keeps its detail and doesn't turn into a bright blur. Use portrait mode only for people standing on the grass, not for the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when guides say the light is especially good for the Town Hall view.

text.access_note: This is a public park, but check the official site before you go for opening times and event days, and ask event staff before photographing at Open Air Theatre events.

name: Old Colombo Dutch Hospital
label: Dutch Hospital
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hospital Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Hospital Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7083723: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Restored 17th-century Dutch building now with restaurants and shops.

text.description: The Old Colombo Dutch Hospital is thought to be the oldest building in the Fort area, and it still looks like a Dutch colonial building. It is believed to have been in use by 1681, when it cared for officers, staff and seafarers of the Dutch East India Company. It later served as an apothecaries' base and a police station, was badly damaged in 1996, and reopened in 2011 as a shopping and dining precinct. Its long, low wings, deep verandas and thick walls make it easy to photograph. The building has five wings around two courtyards, and the walls are about 50 cm thick. Together these give you plenty of repeating arches, shadows and lines to work with. From the street you can take in the whole frontage, with the Fort streetscape around it. Stepping inside the precinct gives you a different picture: a courtyard framed by arched walkways, with greenery. For a quieter angle, walk along Canal Row, where a Dutch-era canal once ran, and photograph the long side wall without the entrance crowds. Keep your phone straight and level so the horizontal roofline and veranda do not slope. Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright. Ask before photographing inside shops or private events.
text.geographic_location: In the Fort district of central Colombo, on Hospital Street, close to the harbour side of the old Dutch-era quarter. Canal Row, a narrow lane, runs along one side of the building.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head into the Fort area and ask for the Dutch Hospital on Hospital Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the full length. Use telephoto (2x or more) for arches, roof details and verandas.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hospital Street (in front of the main façade, facing the building). The colonial-era façade of the old hospital building with the street in the foreground, framed against the surrounding Fort-area streetscape. From here the old hospital sits to the east, with the street in the foreground and the Fort streetscape around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal grid line so the walls stay upright. Keep a little of the street at the bottom to give a sense of place. For something different, try the courtyard in the Dutch Hospital Shopping Precinct, framed by its arched walkways. Or try Canal Row for a quieter side view of the long wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus and lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour. With ultra-wide, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where lines can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows under the verandas. Bright midday sun can make the arches look very contrasty.

text.access_note: The precinct is a shopping and dining area, so access to individual shops and venues may be restricted; check the official site before you go, and ask before photographing inside shops or private events.

name: Pettah Floating Market
label: Floating Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pettah Floating Market' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/303907118: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pettah Floating Market' (341 m across).
notes: Market of floating stalls on Beira Lake.

text.description:
Pettah Floating Market sits on Bastian Mawatha, the street that links Pettah's Central Bus Stand with Colombo Fort railway station. It was built as a tourist market, with 92 stalls, some of them on boats on Beira Lake, selling local produce and handicrafts. It opened on 25 August 2014. One aim was to give street traders a proper place to work, so they were no longer crowding pedestrians off the footpaths in busy Pettah.

For photographs, the appeal is the setting rather than the shopping. The stalls are simple, low and calm in style, and they sit beside the water. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the market, on the lakeside walkways. From here you can take in the pavilions and the water together. For a quieter angle, you can walk to the east end entrance, a short distance away. This is a separate option and not the phone icon on the map.

The market is in decline. Most stalls are reported closed and a redevelopment is under discussion, so aim for the pavilions and the water, not a lively trading scene. The lake water can look murky and smell strong in hot weather, so keep your frames wide and let the reflections and the lines of the walkways do the work. Photography is generally fine, but ask before taking close-up shots of vendors.
text.geographic_location: In Pettah, the busy trading district of central Colombo, on Bastian Mawatha beside Beira Lake. It lies between the Central Bus Stand and Colombo Fort railway station.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops serve this spot, so start from Colombo Fort or Pettah and head for Bastian Mawatha, the street running between the Central Bus Stand and Colombo Fort railway station. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Pettah Floating Market. Once there, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the market. For the quieter angle, you can walk on to the east end entrance, though this is a separate option. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the pavilions, walkways and water together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view, and use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out roof lines and reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a quieter angle, walk to the east end entrance, a separate option, and look back over the pavilions and the water, away from the main entrance crowds. The red-roofed pavilions and wooden walkways over Beira Lake are the main subject from either spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the walkway rails as leading lines that run into the frame, with the pavilions on one side and the water on the other. Keep the horizon level. Leave out any closed stalls that look untidy by framing tight on the roofs and reflections. Ask first if you want a close-up of a person.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pavilions to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and water keep their colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, resting your elbows on the rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset, when the light on the water is warmest.

text.access_note: The market is a public tourist area on the lakeside, but with many stalls reported closed, check locally whether stalls are open before you go.

name: Beira Lake
label: Beira Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Colombo City Centre' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Colombo City Hotel' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Central lake with the skyline reflected in the water.

text.description: Beira Lake is a large, man-made stretch of water in the middle of Colombo, with large businesses and warehouses around its edge. The Portuguese created it as a moat to protect their fort, by joining a stream to the marshy ditch they had dug. It once covered about 1.65 km2 and is now about 0.65 km2, so what you see is a much smaller lake than the original. It photographs best when the light drops. The water is green with algae, which looks dull by day, but at blue hour the lit buildings are reflected on the surface and the whole scene becomes much more atmospheric. Storks, pelicans and monitor lizards live here, so look for birds at the water's edge. From there you look south-east towards the lake, whose central point is about 1.2 km away. If you want a closer, more traditional shot, Seema Malaka, the white temple pavilion on stilts over the water, is a good alternative, with the high-rises rising behind it. Arrive a little before sunset so you can try a few frames as the sky changes. The smell of the lake is strongest in dry weather, so don't be surprised if you notice it near the water.
text.geographic_location: Beira Lake lies in the centre of Colombo, surrounded by large businesses and warehouses, with the Sri Lanka Exhibition and Convention Centre on its waterfront.
text.directions_text: From there, the middle of the lake is about 1.2 km to the south-east. Use the map to follow the streets and the shoreline. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full dusk view across the lake. Try the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out reflections of lit buildings on the water. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky, as it also pulls in foreground clutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Colombo City Centre (looking west across the lake from the building). A dusk view over the Gangaramaya lake toward the city, with the lit buildings reflected in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the far shoreline on the lower third line, leaving the sky and lit skyline above it. Keep the reflections in the frame, as they are the main attraction of this view. For a different shot, Seema Malaka, the white pavilion on stilts over the water, is a good alternative with the high-rises behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit buildings to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lights don't burn out. Switch on night mode if the phone offers it, and brace your elbows on a ledge or railing and hold still until the shot finishes. If glass is in front of you, press the lens close to it to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk, during the blue hour, when the sky still has colour and the city lights are on.

text.access_note: Colombo City Centre is a building and the exact area open to the public for this view is not confirmed, so check with the building before you go; Seema Malaka is a working temple where covered shoulders and knees are expected and an entrance charge may apply, so check the official site before you go.

name: Independence Memorial Hall
label: Independence Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'D. S. Senanayake statue' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'D. S. Senanayake' (pois); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1078848223: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Independence Memorial Hall' (74 m across).

text.description: Independence Memorial Hall is Sri Lanka's national monument to independence from British rule, marking 4 February 1948, when a Ceylonese-elected legislature took full responsibility for government. It stands in Independence Square (once called Torrington Square) in the Cinnamon Gardens, on the spot where the first parliament was opened that day. The building is a raised stone pavilion with rows of columns and carved detail. Its design follows the Magul Maduwa, the royal audience hall of the Kingdom of Kandy, and it was drawn up by a team of eight architects led by Tom Neville Wynne-Jones. At the head of the monument is a statue of D. S. Senanayake, the first prime minister, known as "the Father of the Nation". The hall photographs well because the statue gives you a strong foreground, with the pale pavilion and its columns rising behind it, and the lawns and trees around it soften the frame. It is still used for national day celebrations and other official and religious events, so the front lawns can be fenced off or busy on those days. For an easy set of pictures, start near the statue, then walk slowly around it so the pavilion changes behind it. Keep your phone level so the columns stay straight, and leave a little space around the top of the roofline.
text.geographic_location: The hall is in the Cinnamon Gardens area of Colombo, in Independence Square, which was formerly called Torrington Square.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby, so head for Independence Square in the Cinnamon Gardens and ask for Independence Memorial Hall. The statue is nearby at the head of the monument, so find it by eye. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the pavilion behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole width of the hall and lawns, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved stonework and the columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the hall, at the head of the monument). The statue of the first prime minister in the foreground with the hall's stone pavilion and columns behind it. S. Senanayake statue. The photo shows the first prime minister's statue in the foreground, with the hall's stone pavilion and columns behind it. Walking slowly around the statue helps you show how big the monument is.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the statue on one third of the frame, with the columns filling the rest. Hold the phone level so the verticals stay straight. For a different view, try Independence Avenue, where the raised monument is seen down the avenue with the large flag in front, or a quieter side angle from Independence Square, framed by the lawns and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone does not turn white against the sky. If people are standing in front of the columns, take a few shots, or use Live Photos, and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework and fewer people on the lawns. Avoid national ceremony days if you want a clear view of the statue.

text.access_note: The hall is an active venue for national ceremonies and official events, so the front lawns may be closed on some days, and the museum may have its own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Colombo Lighthouse
label: Colombo Lighthouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Colombo Lighthouse' (6 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/528048970: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Colombo Lighthouse' (6 m across).
notes: Lighthouse on the Fort peninsula near the sea.

text.description:
Colombo Lighthouse is a white cylindrical tower on Galbokka Point, on the waterfront just south of the port. It was built in 1952 and stands 29 metres high on a concrete base about 12 metres tall. Four lion statues guard the foot of the tower, which gives you something close and characterful to photograph. A naval gun battery sits at its base, and the Sri Lanka Navy has used it for traditional gun salutes.

It photographs well because the tower is simple and clean-lined, and from the garden and plaza in front it stands against open sea and sky, with the port and harbour at the edges of the view. Land reclamation for the Port City has left the lighthouse inland of the water, and some visitors find the harbour view partly blocked, so look at the whole scene before choosing your angle.

The phone icon on the map is right at the tower, in the garden and plaza facing the ocean. Sunset is the time guides most often recommend. The tower can be viewed from outside but not climbed. The area is next to Naval Headquarters, and visitors report that photography is restricted in some directions. Look for signs, follow any instructions from staff or guards, and check on site before you shoot. Do not confuse this with the Old Colombo Lighthouse and Clock Tower in Fort, which is a different building.
text.geographic_location: Colombo Lighthouse stands at Galbokka Point on the Colombo Fort waterfront, just south of the Port of Colombo and across the street from Naval Headquarters. It is on Chaithya Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach Colombo Lighthouse on Chaithya Road at Galbokka Point. Make sure you choose this one, not the Old Colombo Lighthouse and Clock Tower near Chatham Street. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so once you arrive there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole white tower against the sea and sky. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the top of the tower will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the lion statues at the base or for ships in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the tower is right beside you, and the sea, sky and the edges of the port and harbour fill the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright on a vertical line so it does not lean. Leave open sea and sky around it. For the ultra-wide shot, hold the phone level and do not tilt it upwards, or the tower will appear to lean backwards. Add a close shot of a lion statue in the foreground for variety. If a sign or guard says not to photograph in a particular direction, respect it and turn to another angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the sky keeps its colour. Check the sky and the tower in the preview before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the time most often recommended by guides and reviews. Arrive a little early so you have time to try a few angles.

text.access_note: The tower can be viewed from outside but not climbed, and it sits in a naval area where photography is restricted in some directions, so check any signs and ask on site before you shoot.

name: St. Lucia's Cathedral
label: St. Lucia's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St. Lucia's Cathedral' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4304782810: the OpenStreetMap point 'St. Lucia Church'.

text.description:
St. Lucia's Cathedral is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Colombo, and it stands in Kotahena, in the north-east of the city. It is considered the oldest and largest parish cathedral in Sri Lanka. The site began with a small place of worship from the Dutch period, and the present building replaced an older church that was in danger of collapsing. Outside, the Renaissance-style facade rests on large Ionic columns and carries seven statues. Above it, the cross on the dome's lantern stands out against the sky. Inside, there are larger-than-life painted saints along the side aisles, carved dark-wood confessionals and white marble altars in the transepts. The stained glass glows when sunlight passes through it.

One of the most impressive views is from the choir loft. Looking down the nave, you see the sanctuary and the Archbishop's episcopal throne, with the decorated interior and the stained glass around it. The narrow stairs to the loft pass a huge bell that weighs 4,300 lbs, and the loft also holds a pipe organ given in 1934. It is a good place for a wide, symmetrical interior photo. Step back outside afterwards for the facade. Scaffolding from restoration work may be in the way of the facade or the interior, so be ready to change your angle. Keep flash off, stay quiet during services, and expect large crowds on Sundays.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in Kotahena, in the north-east of Colombo, on St Lucia's Street. It stands close to St. Benedict's College, which is linked to it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops serve this spot, so start from Kotahena in the north-east of Colombo and make your way to St Lucia's Street. The road up to the cathedral is one-way and can get crowded around school closing time, so arrive earlier or later in the afternoon if you can. Ask your driver to drop you at the cathedral on St Lucia's Street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sanctuary and throne. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the nave and ceiling, and use telephoto (2x or more) for the throne, the statues or a stained-glass window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your photo inside St. Lucia's Cathedral, in the nave, looking down from the choir loft. From there you see the sanctuary below, with the Archbishop's episcopal throne, the decorated interior and the stained glass in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central aisle up with the middle of the frame so the walls stay straight. Keep the throne in the lower half and let the arches fill the top. For a second view, photograph the facade from the front area outside. Its columns, statues and the cross on the dome lantern against the sky all fit in a single frame, and the statue of Mary there is a handy reference point.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Do not use flash. Tap on the brightest window or the throne to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the stained glass keeps its colour. Rest your elbows on the loft rail to keep the phone steady, especially if you use night mode in dim light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A weekday morning, when there are fewer people. Daylight also helps the stained glass glow.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so respect services and quiet, and check the official site or the parish before you go for visiting arrangements and access to the choir loft.

name: Old Parliament Building, Colombo
label: Old Parliament
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Galle Face Green' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Galle Face Green' (way/27712165): edge nearest the subject (978 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/340617005: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Parliament' (79 m across).
notes: Neoclassical building on the seafront next to Galle Face.

text.description:
The Old Parliament Building is a white neoclassical landmark with a long colonnade, standing on the seafront at the northern end of Galle Face. It was built for the Legislative Council of Ceylon and opened on 29 January 1930. It was designed by Austin Woodeson of the Public Works Department. Parliament sat here for 53 years, until the move to the new complex at Sri Jayawardenepura in 1983. Today it houses the Presidential Secretariat, so it is a working government building rather than a museum.

It photographs well because of its symmetry. The row of columns gives a strong, regular pattern, and the open lawn of Galle Face Green in front gives you clean foreground and plenty of sky. From the green you can fit the whole facade in one frame, with the sea air and wide space around it. If you walk to the pavement on the road side, you can also photograph the front garden, which holds bronze statues of statesmen, including D. S. Senanayake, the first Prime Minister of Ceylon.

Keep your photos to the exterior. The inside is closed to visitors, and you should shoot from outside the fence. Rules on photography near the building seem to vary, so check on site, and keep security posts out of your pictures. Drones are reported to be restricted near government buildings, so leave yours at home.
text.geographic_location: In the Fort area of Colombo, at the northern end of Galle Face Green, facing the sea. It is close to the President's House and next to the General Treasury Building.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, train or tram stop nearby, so head for the Fort area or Galle Face Green by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped at the northern end of the green. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade and colonnade framed by the lawn. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the columns, the coat of arms or the statues. Ultra-wide (0.5x) is only worth using if you walk much closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Galle Face Green (northern end of the green, facing the building). The full neoclassical facade and colonnade framed by the open lawn in the foreground, with a wide-angle frame. From there you look north across the open lawn at the whole neoclassical front and its colonnade, with the green filling the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the horizontal lines so the facade sits level. Keep a band of lawn at the bottom and some sky at the top, rather than cropping tight. Hold the phone steady and keep it level. For a second view, go to the pavement on Sir Baron Jayatilleke Mawatha and photograph the facade and the statues in the front garden from across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright walls keep their detail and the sky does not wash out. Skip portrait mode and night mode here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when warm light falls on the columns.

text.access_note: This is the Presidential Secretariat and its interior is closed to the public, so photograph the exterior from outside the fence, and check on site for any photography restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point the building will look fairly small in an ultra-wide (0.5x) frame, so the default lens (1x) or a little zoom works better.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in a bright white facade.

name: Town Hall, Colombo
label: Colombo Town Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Viharamahadevi Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Viharamahadevi Park Aquarium' (node/10107520123): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13887429: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Town Hall, Colombo' (152 m across).
notes: White neoclassical building often called the White House of Colombo.

text.description: Colombo Town Hall is a white, neoclassical building that stands at the head of Viharamahadevi Park, with the lawns running out in front of it. That open space is why it photographs so well from a phone: you can stand back far enough to fit in the long colonnaded front and the dome above it. The main porch has six Corinthian columns, and each column is about 11.6 m tall. The whole building is roughly 108 m long. The design, by S. J. Edwards, won an international competition in 1922 and takes its cue from the Capitol in Washington, D.C. The foundation stone was laid on 24 May 1924 and the building was formally opened on 9 August 1928. It is still the home of the Colombo Municipal Council and the mayor's office, so treat it as a working building and photograph the outside. From the park, look for the symmetry: the central porch, the dome behind it and the matching rows of columns on either side. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the columns upright, and let the grass and fountain fill the lower part of the picture. If a path or a few people walk through the frame, wait a moment and take several shots. A golden Buddha statue in the park also makes a good foreground for a second, different view.
text.geographic_location: In central Colombo, directly in front of Viharamahadevi Park, which is the open green space you shoot across to see the building.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way in is by taxi or hired scooter to Viharamahadevi Park in central Colombo. From there the Town Hall is about 277 m to the east, a short walk if you want to go closer. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the fountain area, which takes in the facade and dome with room to spare. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and the full width no longer fits. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome or the row of columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Viharamahadevi Park (central fountain area, facing the Town Hall facade across the lawns). The full white colonnaded facade and central dome of the Town Hall, framed by the park's open lawns and fountain area. The Town Hall lies to the east, across the lawns. From here the full white colonnaded facade and the central dome are in view, framed by the open grass and the fountain area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the porch and dome on the middle gridline so the two wings balance. Keep the phone upright and level so the columns don't lean. Use some lawn or the fountain as a foreground. For a variation, the golden Buddha statue in the park can sit in the foreground with the Town Hall behind it across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the stonework keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out. Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon and columns straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 9 am, gives soft light on the facade. Late afternoon is also a good choice. Take extra care in the park after dark.

text.access_note: The exterior is easy to see and photograph from Viharamahadevi Park, which is free and open in daylight; the Town Hall is a working government building and its interior is generally closed, so check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside.

name: Wolvendaal Church
label: Wolvendaal Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wolvendaal Church' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/682652569: the OpenStreetMap point 'Wolvendaal Church'.
notes: Dutch Reformed church from the 18th century.

text.description:
Wolvendaal Church sits on a rise in Pettah, and it is one of the most important Dutch colonial-era buildings in Sri Lanka and one of the oldest Protestant churches still in use. Its foundations were laid in 1749 under the Dutch East India Company (VOC), and it was dedicated for worship on 6 March 1757. The name means 'Wolf's Dale'. The Dutch took the jackals roaming the marshy ground here for wolves. The church is built in a plain Doric style on a Greek-cross plan, with walls nearly 1.5 m thick and a tall central roof that looks like a dome. It is still used for worship today.

For a phone photo, start at the old gates on the church boundary. They carry the VOC emblem, and the white church stands behind them. This gives you a tighter, more personal picture than the full frontage. Fill the lower half of the frame with the gate detail and let the church sit softly behind it.

If you want the whole building, step back along the Wolvendaal Street frontage and photograph the white facade, dome and red roof together. Inside, the nave has tall windows, old pews, the oldest organ in Sri Lanka and engraved tombstones set into the floor. Interior photos are not guaranteed. Ask permission first, especially during a service, and if the church is closed, stay with the exterior views. The exterior may also look a little weathered compared with older photos.
text.geographic_location: Wolvendaal Church is in Pettah, a neighbourhood of Colombo, just outside the old Fort area. It stands on a rise, with original VOC gates at the church boundary.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Pettah and head for Wolvendaal Church by taxi or hired scooter. Ask your driver to drop you at the church gates. Once you are there, the phone icon on the map is at the church boundary, right by the old gates. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate and emblem with the church behind. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter crop of the emblem, or use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are inside and need the whole nave.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows a close detail of the old gate with the Dutch East India Company (VOC) logo, and the church behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Fill the foreground with the gate and emblem, and keep the church in the background. Turn on gridlines and place the emblem on a third, with the white building filling the rest. For an alternative, step back along the Wolvendaal Street frontage to capture the whole white facade, dome and red roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the emblem to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail. Portrait mode can soften the church behind the gate, but check that the gate edges stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls. On Sundays, services are held, so expect worshippers and be discreet with your camera.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship with services on Sundays, so ask before taking photos inside. The church may be closed, so be ready to stay with the exterior views.

name: Seema Malaka
label: Seema Malaka
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Seema Malaka' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q24239464: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Floating Buddhist meditation hall on Beira Lake.

text.description:
Seema Malaka is a Buddhist temple that sits right on Beira Lake, reached by walkways from the shore. It is used mainly for meditation and rest rather than for worship, which gives it a calm feel even though it is in the middle of the city. The temple stands on three platforms over the water, linked to the mainland and to each other by pontoon bridges. The main roof is covered in blue tiles, and the timber handrails and pavilions have a Kandyan look. The platforms hold many seated Buddha statues, each showing a different hand gesture. One side platform has a Bodhi tree grown from a branch of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura.

The temple was first built in the late 19th century, but the original structure slowly sank into the water in the 1970s. In 1976 the Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa redesigned and rebuilt it, and that is the temple you see today.

It photographs well because the buildings, statues and water all fit in one frame. For a quieter view than the main platform, walk to the lake shore at the foot of the walkway and look out at the temple with the water in front of it. Once you are on the platforms, the seated Buddha statues along the edge make a good foreground, with the timber pavilions and the lake behind. Keep a respectful distance from anyone praying or meditating.
text.geographic_location: Seema Malaka stands in Beira Lake in central Colombo, a few hundred metres east of Gangaramaya Temple and about 2 kilometres south-east of Galle Face Green.
text.directions_text: No train station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The temple is about 2 kilometres south-east of Galle Face Green and a few hundred metres east of Gangaramaya Temple, on Beira Lake. From the shore, the temple is reached by a narrow walkway over the water. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple and the lake together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the platforms and water, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for Buddha statues and roof details from the shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the temple sitting on the water with the lake in the foreground, a quieter angle than the main platform. A second option is on the platform itself, where the seated Buddha statues along the edge frame the timber pavilions and the lake behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the temple along one of the lines, leaving the water in the foreground. Keep the horizon level so the platforms do not look tilted. From the platform, put a Buddha statue in the foreground and let the pavilions and lake fill the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the blue roof and the sky keep their colour. Use portrait mode for a close shot of a statue, and hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a calmer lake.

text.access_note: Photography is generally allowed, but you should remove your shoes before the platforms, cover your shoulders and knees, and never pose with your back to a Buddha statue; check on the day whether there is an entry fee.
